style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: Chapter 17 is a string of single-verse proverbs with no one storyline, yet certain threads keep returning -- the peace of a quiet household over a feast spoiled by strife (vv. 1, 14, 19), the LORD who refines and weighs the heart while men refine mere metal (v. 3), the corrosive power of the bribe and the perverting of justice (vv. 8, 15, 23, 26), and above all the contrast between the wise man and the fool, whose folly grieves his parents (vv. 21, 25), wastes his money (v. 16), and is only ever hidden by silence (vv. 27-28). Running through it all is the theme of speech and restraint: the man of knowledge guards his words, and even a fool seems wise when he holds his peace.

1.text: Better a dry crust of bread eaten in quiet than a house heaped with feasting and full of strife.
1.amp: Better [tov -- good, the thing more worth having] a dry morsel and quietness [shalvah -- untroubled calm] with it, than a house [bayith] full of feasting [zebach -- literally sacrifices, hence festal meat] with strife [riyb -- quarreling, the language of a lawsuit].
1.notes: tov (H2896) frames the whole 'better-than' proverb; the contrast is not poverty versus wealth but peace versus quarreling. zebach (H2077) is sacrificial meat -- the abundance of a feast day -- yet a feast soured by riyb (H7379), domestic litigation, is worth less than a bare crust in shalvah (H7962).

2.text: A servant who acts with skill will come to rule over a son who brings shame, and will share the inheritance among the brothers as one of them.
2.amp: A servant [ebed] who deals wisely [sakal -- acts with prudent skill, and so prospers] will rule [mashal -- have dominion, govern] over a son [ben] who brings shame [bosh], and will have a share [chalaq -- be allotted a portion] of the inheritance [nachalah] among the brothers [achim].
2.notes: sakal (H7919) joins insight to success -- skill that actually produces good outcomes. The proverb overturns the expected order of birth: character, not bloodline, decides who governs and who inherits, so that a wise ebed (H5650) can be raised over a shameful ben (H1121) and given a nachalah (H5159) among the sons (cf. Gen 15:2-3).

3.text: The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, but it is the LORD who assays the heart.
3.amp: The refining pot [mitsreph -- the smelter's crucible] is for silver [keseph], and the furnace for gold [zahab], but the LORD [YHWH] tests [bachan -- assays, proves by fire] the hearts.
3.notes: bachan (H974) is the metallurgist's word for testing metal in the fire to expose what it truly is. As the mitsreph (H4715) burns silver down to its purity, so the LORD applies His own refining heat to the human heart, knowing it as no furnace can (cf. Mal 3:3; Jer 17:10).

4.text: An evildoer listens eagerly to wicked lips, and a liar lends his ear to a destroying tongue.
4.amp: A doer of evil [raa] gives heed [qashab -- listens intently, leans in] to false [aven -- iniquitous] lips [saphah]; and a liar [sheqer] gives ear [azan] to a ruinous [havvah -- engulfing, destructive] tongue [lashon].
4.notes: qashab (H7181), the same alert listening Proverbs urges toward wisdom, here bends toward evil -- a man's ear reveals his heart. The wicked are drawn to the speech that matches them: aven (H205) lips and a havvah (H1942) tongue, words that crave and devour, find their natural audience in the sheqer (H8267) man.

5.text: Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker; whoever gloats over disaster will not go unpunished.
5.amp: Whoever mocks the poor [rush -- the destitute] reproaches his Maker [asah -- the One who made him]; and he who is glad [sameach] at calamity [eyd -- sudden ruin] shall not go unpunished [naqah -- will not be held innocent].
5.notes: to scorn the poor man is to scorn the God who made him (asah, H6213), for both rich and poor bear the same Maker's stamp (cf. 14:31; 22:2). Gloating over another's eyd (H343) likewise invites judgment: the verb naqah (H5352) means to be acquitted, and the mocker will not be.

6.text: An old man wears his children's children as a crown, and a child finds his splendor in the parents who came before him.
6.amp: Children's children are the crown [atarah -- the wreath of honor] of old men [zaqen]; and the glory [tipheret -- splendor, beauty] of children [banim] are their fathers [avot].
6.notes: the atarah (H5850) is a victor's or honoree's wreath -- a long line of descendants is the visible reward of an old man's life. The proverb runs both ways: the aged are crowned by their grandchildren, and the young find their tipheret (H8597) in honorable parents, binding the generations in mutual honor.

7.text: Fine, lofty speech ill suits a fool -- how much less do lying lips suit a noble.
7.amp: Excellent [yether -- abundant, lofty] speech [saphah] is not fitting [naveh -- comely, becoming] for a fool [naval -- the morally senseless]; how much less are lying [sheqer] lips fitting for a prince [nadiv -- a noble, one of generous and honorable rank].
7.notes: the proverb pairs two mismatches. Grand words sit as oddly on a naval (H5036) -- the boorish, godless fool -- as falsehood sits on a nadiv (H5081), whose very name (from 'willing, generous') marks him as one bound to noble truthfulness. Each kind of speech betrays or befits the speaker's character.

8.text: A bribe seems a charmed stone in the eyes of the one who gives it -- wherever he turns, he thinks it makes him prosper.
8.amp: A gift [shochad -- a bribe] is like a precious [chen -- a stone of grace, a charm] stone [even] in the eyes of its owner [baal]; wherever it turns, it succeeds [sakal -- gets results, prospers].
8.notes: the verse describes, without endorsing, how a bribe looks to the man who wields it -- like a magic 'stone of grace' (chen, H2580) that opens every door. The same root sakal (H7919) that names true skill in v.2 here names the bribe's apparent effectiveness; the briber trusts it as a charm, though Scripture condemns the practice (cf. v.23; Ex 23:8).

9.text: Whoever covers an offense seeks love, but whoever keeps bringing the matter up divides close friends.
9.amp: He who covers [kasah -- conceals, draws a veil over] a transgression [pesha -- rebellion, offense] seeks [baqash] love [ahavah]; but he who repeats [shanah -- harps on, brings up again] a matter [dabar] separates [parad -- splits apart] close friends [alluph -- intimate companions].
9.notes: to kasah (H3680) an offense is not to excuse sin but to refuse to broadcast it, and so to pursue ahavah (H160). The opposite is the one who keeps reopening the wound -- repeating the dabar (H1697) -- and so drives a wedge (parad, H6504) between the dearest of friends (cf. 10:12; 1 Pet 4:8).

10.text: A single rebuke cuts deeper into a discerning man than a hundred blows into a fool.
10.amp: A rebuke [gearah -- a sharp reproof] sinks deeper [nachath -- enters and presses down] into one who understands [biyn -- the discerning] than a hundred stripes [makkah -- blows] into a fool [kesil -- the dull, stubborn fool].
10.notes: the proverb measures teachability. A word of gearah (H1606) reaches further into the heart of the discerning (biyn, H995) than a hundred beatings reach into the kesil (H3684); the wise are corrected by a sentence, the fool not even by a flogging (cf. 27:22).

11.text: The evil man pursues nothing but rebellion -- so a cruel messenger will be sent against him.
11.amp: An evil [ra] man seeks [baqash] only rebellion [meri -- defiant revolt]; therefore a cruel [akzari -- merciless] messenger [malak] shall be sent [shalach] against him.
11.notes: meri (H4805) is settled, defiant rebellion -- the man does not stumble into evil but actively seeks (baqash, H1245) it. The reckoning is fitting: a malak (H4397), here a human envoy or agent of justice, akzari (H394) and without pity, is dispatched against the rebel who would show no mercy himself.

12.text: Better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in the grip of his folly.
12.amp: Let a bear [dob] robbed of her whelps meet a man [ish] -- rather that than [al -- by no means] a fool [kesil] in his folly [ivvelet -- raging stupidity].
12.notes: the most dangerous animal a traveler could face was a she-bear bereaved of her cubs (cf. 2 Sam 17:8), yet the proverb judges her less perilous than a kesil (H3684) loosed in his ivvelet (H200). The bear acts from instinct and is done; the fool's folly is reasonless, unpredictable, and without limit.

13.text: If a man returns evil for good, evil will never leave his house.
13.amp: Whoever returns [shub -- pays back, repays] evil [ra] for good [tov], evil [ra] shall not depart [mush -- move away, withdraw] from his house [bayith].
13.notes: to repay tov (H2896) with ra (H7451) is a violation so deep it summons lasting consequence: the same evil he dealt out will mush (H4185) -- refuse to budge -- from his own bayith (H1004). The proverb warns that ingratitude poisons not only a relationship but a household's whole future.

14.text: Starting a quarrel is like breaching a dam -- so drop the dispute before it bursts out.
14.amp: The beginning [reshith] of strife [madon -- contention] is like one releasing water [breaching a dam]; therefore leave off [natash -- abandon, let go of] contention [riyb] before it breaks out [galash / gala -- bursts, is exposed].
14.notes: reshith (H7225), the opening trickle of strife, is pictured as the first seep through an earthen dam -- harmless for a moment, then unstoppable. The counsel is to natash (H5203), to walk away from the riyb (H7379), while the breach is still small; once the wall goes, no one controls the flood (cf. v.1).

15.text: Acquitting the guilty and condemning the innocent -- the LORD detests them both alike.
15.amp: He who justifies [tsadaq -- declares righteous] the wicked [rasha], and he who condemns [rasha (verb) -- declares guilty] the just [tsaddiq], both alike are an abomination [toevah] to the LORD [YHWH].
15.notes: the verse turns on a deliberate play: the same root underlies tsadaq (H6663, to declare righteous) and the condemning of the tsaddiq (H6662). To reverse the verdicts of justice -- freeing the rasha (H7563), damning the righteous -- is a toevah (H8441), something the LORD holds in active disgust (cf. Isa 5:23; Deut 25:1).

16.text: What good is money in a fool's hand to buy wisdom, when he has no heart to learn it?
16.amp: Why is there a price [mechir -- purchase money] in the hand of a fool [kesil] to buy [qanah -- acquire, get] wisdom [chokmah], seeing he has no heart [leb -- mind and will] for it?
16.notes: wisdom cannot be purchased by one who does not want it. Though the kesil (H3684) hold the full mechir (H4242) and could 'buy' chokmah (H2451), he lacks the leb (H3820) -- the inner desire and understanding -- that alone receives it. The means are useless without the will (cf. v.10).

17.text: A friend loves at every season, and a brother is born for the day of trouble.
17.amp: A friend [rea -- companion, neighbor] loves [ahav] at all times [et -- in every season], and a brother [ach] is born [yalad] for adversity [tsarah -- distress, the tight place].
17.notes: the proverb sets steady friendship and brotherhood side by side, not in contrast: the rea (H7453) loves through every et (H6256), and the ach (H251) is, as it were, born (yalad, H3205) precisely for the hour of tsarah (H6869). True kinship proves itself not in ease but in the narrow, pressing place of trouble.

18.text: A man without sense strikes hands in pledge, putting up security for his neighbor.
18.amp: A man [adam] lacking sense [leb -- literally void of heart] strikes hands [taqa -- claps the hand to seal a deal] and becomes surety [arav -- gives a guarantee, takes on another's debt] in the presence of his friend [rea].
18.notes: to 'strike hands' (taqa, H8628) was to seal a binding pledge with a handshake. The man void of leb (H3820) rashly makes himself arav (H6148) -- legally liable for his neighbor's debt -- a recurring warning in Proverbs against backing obligations one cannot cover (cf. 6:1-5; 11:15).

19.text: Whoever loves an offense loves a fight; whoever builds his gate high is courting ruin.
19.amp: He who loves [ahav] transgression [pesha -- offense, rebellion] loves strife [matsah -- quarreling]; he who raises high [gabah -- exalts, makes lofty] his gate [petach -- doorway, entrance] seeks [baqash] destruction [sheber -- breaking, ruin].
19.notes: the two halves interpret each other. To love pesha (H6588) is to love matsah (H4683), the conflict it breeds. The lofty gate is likely pride made visible -- the man who gabah (H1361), lifting his doorway above his neighbors in arrogant display, is in truth building toward his own sheber (H7667), the collapse pride invites (cf. 16:18; 18:12).

20.text: A man with a crooked heart finds no good, and one with a twisted tongue falls into trouble.
20.amp: He who has a crooked [iqqesh -- bent, perverse] heart [leb] finds [matsa] no good [tov]; and he who has a perverse [haphak -- turned, inverted] tongue [lashon] falls [naphal] into mischief [ra -- evil, calamity].
20.notes: the verse pairs heart and tongue, root and fruit. A leb (H3820) that is iqqesh (H6141), bent out of true, never finds the tov (H2896) it grasps at; and a lashon (H3956) that is haphak (H2015) -- speech that turns truth upside down -- ends by toppling (naphal, H5307) its owner into the very ra (H7451) he spoke.

21.text: Whoever fathers a fool does so to his sorrow; the father of a senseless son has no joy.
21.amp: He who begets [yalad] a fool [kesil] does it to his grief [tugah -- sorrow, heaviness]; and the father [av] of a fool [naval -- the morally senseless] has no joy [samach -- gladness].
21.notes: this proverb opens a small cluster on the cost of a foolish child (cf. v.25; 10:1). To bring forth (yalad, H3205) a kesil (H3684) is to give birth to lifelong tugah (H8424); the av (H1) of a naval (H5036) is robbed of the samach (H8055), the simple parental gladness, that a wise child brings.

22.text: A cheerful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.
22.amp: A merry [sameach -- glad, joyful] heart [leb] does good like a medicine [gehah -- a cure, healing]; but a broken [nake -- stricken, crushed] spirit [ruach] dries up [yabesh -- withers] the bones.
22.notes: Proverbs knows the body answers to the soul. A sameach (H8056) heart works like gehah (H1456), a healing remedy, while a nake (H5218) ruach (H7307) -- a spirit beaten down -- saps the very marrow, drying the bones (cf. 15:13; 18:14). Inner joy and inner despair are written into the frame.

23.text: The wicked man slips a bribe from the fold of his robe to bend the course of justice.
23.amp: A wicked [rasha] man takes [laqach] a gift [shochad -- a bribe] out of the bosom [cheq -- the fold of the garment, where it is hidden] to pervert [natah -- bend, turn aside] the ways [orach] of judgment [mishpat -- justice].
23.notes: the bribe of v.8, seen now from the side of corruption. The rasha (H7563) receives the shochad (H7810) secretly, drawn from the hidden cheq (H2436) of his robe, precisely in order to natah (H5186) -- to bend the straight orach (H734) of mishpat (H4941) off its line. Justice is not denied openly but quietly purchased.

24.text: Wisdom is right before the face of the discerning, but the eyes of a fool roam to the ends of the earth.
24.amp: Wisdom [chokmah] is before the face [panim] of him who has understanding [biyn -- the discerning]; but the eyes [ayin] of a fool [kesil] are on the ends [qatseh -- the far edges] of the earth [eretz].
24.notes: the discerning man keeps chokmah (H2451) directly before his panim (H6440) -- near at hand, the fixed object of his gaze -- and so finds it. The kesil (H3684), by contrast, lets his eyes wander to the qatseh (H7097) of the earth, chasing every distant fancy, and so never sees the wisdom standing in front of him (cf. Eccl 2:14).

25.text: A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to the mother who bore him.
25.amp: A foolish [kesil] son [ben] is a grief [kaas -- vexation, provocation] to his father [av], and bitterness [memer -- bitter sorrow] to her who bore [yalad] him.
25.notes: the companion to v.21, now naming both parents. The kesil (H3684) son is kaas (H3708) -- a galling vexation -- to his av (H1), and memer (H4470), sheer bitterness, to the mother who gave him birth (yalad, H3205). Folly wounds the two who love the child most.

26.text: To fine the innocent is not good, nor to flog the noble for doing right.
26.amp: Also to punish [anash -- fine, impose a penalty on] the just [tsaddiq] is not good [tov], nor to strike [nakah -- flog, beat] princes [nadiv -- nobles] for uprightness [yosher -- doing what is right].
26.notes: a miscarriage of justice in the opposite direction from v.23: not letting the guilty off but penalizing the righteous. To anash (H6064) the tsaddiq (H6662) or nakah (H5221) the honorable man for his yosher (H3476) overturns the moral order -- punishing the very integrity that ought to be honored (cf. v.15).

27.text: Whoever has knowledge holds back his words, and a man of understanding keeps a cool, even spirit.
27.amp: He who has [yada -- knows, possesses] knowledge [daat] restrains [chasak -- holds back, spares] his words [emer]; and a man [ish] of understanding [tebunah] is of a cool [qar -- cold, calm] spirit [ruach].
27.notes: true daat (H1847) shows itself in restraint: the knowing man chasak (H2820) -- reins in -- his speech. The marginal sense behind 'excellent' is qar (H7119), cool: the man of tebunah (H8394) keeps a calm, unheated ruach (H7307), the opposite of the hot-tempered fool (cf. 14:29; Jas 1:19).

28.text: Even a fool, when he stays silent, is reckoned wise; when he keeps his lips shut, he is thought discerning.
28.amp: Even a fool [evil -- the senseless one], when he holds his peace [charash -- keeps silent], is counted [chashab -- reckoned, accounted] wise [chakam]; and he who shuts [atam -- closes, stops up] his lips [saphah] is esteemed discerning [biyn].
28.notes: the chapter's closing irony, sealing the theme of restrained speech (vv. 9, 14, 27). Even the evil (H191) is chashab (H2803) -- reckoned -- chakam (H2450) while he charash (H2790), holds his tongue; to atam (H331) the lips is to pass for biyn (H995). Silence cannot make a fool wise, but it can keep him from proving he is not (cf. Job 13:5).
